The guidance specifies additional GM-BSL2 laboratory-facility features.

WHO LBM4 uses an evidence- and risk-based approach in which safety measures are balanced against the actual risk of the activity on a case-by-case basis.
Risk assessment requires information on biological hazards, procedures, equipment, facility and human competency; knowledge gaps negatively affect evaluation and control selection.
Risk evaluation considers how exposure/release could occur, likelihood, consequences and whether risks can be controlled to an acceptable level.

WHO's 2024 laboratory biosecurity guidance applies a risk- and evidence-based approach to biosecurity, including governance, secure handling, transport/storage and high-consequence research risk management.

WHO LBM4 includes dedicated guidance on decontamination and waste management; BioSafe should use it as authoritative international corroboration where Malaysian requirements do not fully specify technical practice.

original_claim.text: WHO describes biological risk assessment as a systematic process of gathering information and evaluating risks to support risk management. The results of the assessment inform selection of risk control measures, including training and appropriate PPE.

original_claim.text: In laboratory biosafety, WHO describes a biological hazard as a biological agent whose pathogenic characteristics give it the potential to cause harm to people, animals and/or the environment.
original_claim.verification_status: Verified against WHO Risk Assessment monograph

original_claim.text: WHO defines biological risk in context as the combination of the likelihood that an exposure to or release of a biological hazard occurs during laboratory work and the severity of the consequences if that incident occurs.
original_claim.verification_status: Verified against WHO Risk Assessment monograph

original_claim.text: WHO notes that laboratory biological risk depends on dynamic factors including the procedures performed, equipment available, pathogenic properties of the biological agent, host range, population susceptibility and the competency of laboratory personnel.

original_claim.text: WHO places PPE within broader laboratory biosafety core requirements rather than treating PPE as a complete safety determination. Core requirements include good microbiological practice and procedure, with PPE such as laboratory coats, footwear, gloves and eye protection used as applicable.

WHO indicates that some PPE needs are determined by risk assessment; for example, respiratory protection for biological agents is not a general core requirement and becomes a heightened control measure when the risk assessment indicates it is needed.

WHO's risk-based framework does not use PPE alone to establish that an activity is safe: risk assessment determines the control measures needed for the activity, and control selection can include training, PPE, equipment and other containment measures appropriate to the identified risk.
